reconcile.connective: The leading harmonization reads the two figures as ordinary content versus brim-full capacity — 2,000 baths in normal use, 3,000 when filled to the top.

discrepancy.connective: C. Dennis McKinsey catalogues this as a plain numerical error, noting the same account gives 2,000 baths in Kings and 3,000 in Chronicles with no reconciling qualifier in the text.

skeptic.name: C. Dennis McKinsey
skeptic.attribution: C. Dennis McKinsey (d. 2009), The Encyclopedia of Biblical Errancy (Prometheus Books, 1995)

excerpts.excerpt_text: If it were filled to the brim, it would hold 3000 baths (as here, Ch2 4:5), but ordinarily there were only 2000 baths in it, Kg1 7:26.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly harmonizes the two capacities: 3000 = brim-full, 2000 = ordinary content. The single cleanest both-true statement of the leading reconciliation; parity-capped at one to match the discrepancy pole's named-skeptic unit on this discrepancy_first row.

pd_work.resource: John W. Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John W. Haley
pd_work.note: Haley treats this passage directly, arguing the Sea ordinarily held 2,000 baths but received and held 3,000 when filled to capacity, resting the distinction on the added verb in 2 Chronicles 4:5.

link.note: No dedicated page on an allowlisted apologetics domain (gotquestions.org / carm.org / defendinginerrancy.com) was confirmed for this specific contradiction; link omitted rather than fabricated.
